questions.question_text: Which of the following brain stimulation treatments is U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved for the treatment of depression?

options.text: Focal electrically administered seizure therapy (FEAST).
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS).
Magnetic seizure therapy (MST).
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS).
Deep brain stimulation (DBS).

questions.explanation: The FDA has approved one device for administering repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for the treatment of depression in adult patients who have failed to achieve satisfactory improvement from one previous antidepressant medication. Focal electrically administered seizure therapy (FEAST) is an experimental form of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) that uses direct current to initiate a focal seizure. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), which uses electrical stimulation of peripheral nerves to block pain signals, was grandfathered in by the FDA for treatment of pain conditions, but it has not been rigorously tested for the treatment of depression. Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) uses magnetic fields to initiate seizures. Although MST is promising in terms of causing fewer acute cognitive side effects than traditional ECT, it does not yet have adequate clinical data and remains an experimental treatment for depression. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has a humanitarian device exemption for use in conjunction with medications for the treatment of treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder. Despite promising preliminary data in patients with treatment-resistant depression, DBS does not have FDA approval for this condition.

questions.question_text: How do the antidepressant effects and safety of daily left prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for 3-6 weeks compare with those of psychopharmacological treatments for depression?

options.text: rTMS has a substantially greater risk of seizures.
Effect sizes are consistently smaller for rTMS.
rTMS had comparable efficacy, but the benefits typically abated soon after the course of treatment ended.
rTMS has been shown to be effective in 'real-world' patients with treatment-resistant depression.
High rates of patient discontinuation of rTMS limit its applicability in real-world populations.

correct_answer.text: rTMS has been shown to be effective in 'real-world' patients with treatment-resistant depression.

correct_answers.text: rTMS has been shown to be effective in 'real-world' patients with treatment-resistant depression.

questions.explanation: Studies of TMS in real-world clinical practice settings have highlighted its effectiveness in patients with treatment-resistant depression (Carpenter et al. 2012). In addition, industry-independent clinical studies (George et al. 2010; Mantovani et al. 2012; McDonald et al. 2011) have demonstrated that left prefrontal TMS daily for 3–6 weeks has antidepressant effects that are significantly greater than sham, and that these effects are clinically meaningful (30% remission rate). Even more importantly, the outcomes are at least as robust as those for the next-best choice of antidepressant medication; the procedure was found to be safe and well tolerated, with a low incidence of treatment discontinuation; and the therapeutic effects, once obtained, are reasonably durable. Effect sizes for left prefrontal rTMS are of similar or greater magnitude compared with those observed with the majority of currently approved antidepressant medication treatments (Demitrack and Thase 2009; O’Reardon et al. 2007). The estimated risk of seizure associated with TMS under ordinary clinical use is approximately 1 in 30,000 treatments (0.003% of treatments) or 1 in 1,000 patients (0.1% of patients). This risk is less than or comparable to the risk of seizure associated with antidepressant medications.

questions.question_text: A typical initial course of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) involves administration ___ times per week for a total of ___ treatments?

options.text: Two times per week for a total of 9–12 treatments.
Three times per week for a total of 12–16 treatments.
Two to three times per week for a total of 8–12 treatments.
Two to three times per week for a total of 16–18 treatments.
Four to five times per week for a total of 16–18 treatments.

correct_answer.text: Two to three times per week for a total of 8–12 treatments.

correct_answers.text: Two to three times per week for a total of 8–12 treatments.

questions.explanation: For a typical series or a course of ECT, treatments are usually given two to three times per week for 8–12 treatments. This course may then be followed by maintenance treatment in the form of medication, additional ECT given at less frequent intervals, or both.

questions.question_text: Approximately how strong a magnetic field is typically used in transcranial magnetic stimulation?

options.text: 0.5 Tesla.
1.5 Tesla.
4 Tesla.
7 Tesla.
10 Tesla.

questions.explanation: The electricity flowing in an electromagnetic coil on the scalp creates an extremely potent (near 1.5-Tesla) but brief (microseconds) magnetic field.

questions.question_text: Which of the following aspects of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been useful for researchers studying the brain?

options.text: Repetitive TMS over a brain region can cause a temporary augmentation of a brain function controlled by that region.
Paired-pulse TMS can demonstrate the behavior of local interneurons in the motor cortex and indirectly measure serotonin activity.
Brain circuit excitation caused by TMS reverts to baseline when stimulation ends.
There is no evidence that TMS can induce neurogenesis, which can confound the collection of functional data.
TMS can be conducted in a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine.

correct_answer.text: TMS can be conducted in a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine.

correct_answers.text: TMS can be conducted in a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine.

questions.explanation: TMS can be performed within a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner, which is itself a huge magnet and is constantly on (Bohning 2000; Bohning et al. 1998). One of the more interesting rTMS effects is that for brief periods of time, during stimulation, rTMS can block or inhibit a brain function. That is, rTMS over the motor area that controls speech can temporarily leave the patient speechless (motor aphasia), but only while the device is firing. Additionally, two pulses of TMS in quick succession can provide information about the underlying excitability of a region of cortex. This diagnostic technique, called paired-pulse TMS, can demonstrate the behavior of local interneurons in the motor cortex and serve as an indirect measure of -aminobutyric acid (GABA) or glutamate (Heide et al. 2006). Single nerve cells form themselves into functioning circuits over time through repeated discharges. Externally stimulating a single nerve cell with low-frequency electrical stimulation can cause longterm depression, where the efficiency of links between cells diminishes. Highfrequency stimulation over time can cause the opposite effect, called long-term potentiation. These behaviors are thought to be involved in learning, memory, and dynamic brain changes associated with networks. Many TMS studies have now shown inhibition or excitation lasting for up to several hours beyond the time of stimulation (Di Lazzaro et al. 2005). Animal studies have found that TMS can induce neurogenesis (Pope and Keck 2001).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and seizures?

options.text: The site of stimulation is not significant in terms of the risk of a seizure.
Concurrent use of medications plays no role in seizure risk.
TMS intensity and frequency have no impact on the risk of a seizure.
The estimated risk of a seizure in ordinary clinical use is approximately 10%.
All TMS seizures have occurred during stimulation rather than later.

correct_answer.text: All TMS seizures have occurred during stimulation rather than later.

correct_answers.text: All TMS seizures have occurred during stimulation rather than later.

questions.explanation: TMS pulses applied in rhythmic succession are referred to as repetitive TMS (rTMS). rTMS can create behaviors that do not occur with single pulses, including the potential risk of causing an unintended seizure, particularly if the stimulation is conducted near the motor cortex. Over 20 seizures have occurred in the history of TMS use, out of an unclear total number of people stimulated but easily over 100,000 sessions (Rossi et al. 2009). Since market introduction of the NeuroStar TMS Therapy system in October 2008, seven seizures have been reported with NeuroStar TMS Therapy, over a usage of more than 250,000 treatment sessions and over 8,000 patients. In five of the seven seizures, patients had concurrent use of medications that may have altered the seizure threshold. The estimated risk of seizure under ordinary clinical use is approximately 1 in 30,000 treatments (0.003% of treatments) or 1 in 1,000 patients (0.1% of patients) (M. Demitrack, Neuronetics, personal communication, November 12, 2012). This risk is less than or comparable to the risk of seizure associated with antidepressant medications. All TMS seizures have occurred during stimulation, rather than later, and have been self-limited with no sequelae. rTMS seizures are more likely to occur with certain combinations of TMS intensity, frequency, duration, and interstimulus interval (Wassermann 1997).

questions.question_text: How do functional brain changes seen in depressed patients after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) compare with changes seen in depressed patients after transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)?

options.text: ECT increases global activity following the seizure.
TMS increases limbic activity.
Both TMS and ECT decrease limbic activity.
ECT increases prefrontal activity following the seizure.
No changes in brain activity are seen after TMS stimulation.

questions.explanation: In contrast to imaging studies with ECT that have found that ECT shuts off global and regional activity following the seizure (Nobler et al. 2001), most studies using serial scans in depressed patients undergoing TMS have found increased activity in the cingulate and other limbic regions (Teneback et al. 1999).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is true?

options.text: The costs and inconvenience of tDCS are major obstacles to its wider use.
tDCS's most promising effects have been observed in depression studies.
tDCS affects neuronal excitability by causing neurons to fire at particular frequencies.
tDCS is a relatively safe treatment that can be administered in a patient's home.
In tDCS, the motor threshold is used to titrate dosage.

correct_answer.text: tDCS is a relatively safe treatment that can be administered in a patient's home.

correct_answers.text: tDCS is a relatively safe treatment that can be administered in a patient's home.

questions.explanation: tDCS is a brain stimulation technique achieved through application of constant weak (typically 1 mA) electrical current through scalp electrodes. Unlike transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), tDCS does not elicit action potentials in cortical neurons. Instead, the constant direct current of tDCS induces subthreshold changes in membrane potential that increase or decrease the ease with which an action potential may be triggered (Leung et al. 2009). There are currently no U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–approved therapeutic uses for tDCS. Nevertheless, tDCS remains an active area of research because of the ease with which it can be applied and the flexibility derived from its various potential electrode placements. A small current source and damp sponges (electrodes) are all that is required for tDCS administration. This portable, safe, inexpensive setup is particularly alluring because it may enable tDCS to be used in nontraditional ways, including in a patient’s home or during therapeutic interventions such as cognitive-behavioral therapy or rehabilitation exercises. Thus far, the most promising effects of tDCS have been found in rehabilitation studies. Although more research is needed, there is emerging evidence that tDCS may enhance poststroke aphasia rehabilitation therapies. Appropriate dosing of tDCS remains an unresolved issue. Unlike transcranial magnetic stimulation, which can be titrated based on motor threshold, tDCS is not typically tailored for each individual patient.

questions.question_text: How is vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) thought to impact neuropsychiatric disorders?

options.text: By blocking efferent motor and autonomic signals.
By modulating afferent fibers.
By directly increasing parasympathetic tone.
By initiating seizures.
By altering neuronal excitability.

questions.explanation: The vagus nerve is composed of about 80% afferent sensory fibers carrying information to the brain from the head, neck, thorax, and abdomen (Foley and Dubois 1937). VNS offers the potential for modulating and modifying function in many brain regions, through transsynaptic connections (George et al. 2000). The incoming sensory (afferent) connections of the vagus nerve provide direct projections to many of the brain regions implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. These connections provide a basis for understanding how VNS might be a portal to the brain stem and connected limbic and cortical regions. These pathways likely account for the neuropsychiatric effects of VNS.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about relapse after symptom remission in response to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is true?

options.text: Most patients who experience symptom remission in response to ECT will relapse after 6 months.
Remission is typically maintained for at least 12 months.
Medication does not affect the relapse rate after symptom remission with ECT.
A robust body of evidence shows that maintenance ECT prevents relapse.
ECT is the most effective treatment for both acute and chronic depression.

correct_answer.text: Most patients who experience symptom remission in response to ECT will relapse after 6 months.

correct_answers.text: Most patients who experience symptom remission in response to ECT will relapse after 6 months.

questions.explanation: Although ECT is the most effective acute treatment for depression, it is disappointing that at 6 months, many ECT patients who have responded or remitted will relapse. For example, one study randomly assigned ECT remitters to placebo, nortriptyline, or nortriptyline plus lithium after patients had remitted (Sackeim et al. 2002). At 6 months, the relapse rate was 84% with placebo, 60% with nortriptyline, and 39% with nortriptyline plus lithium. Some psychiatrists administer maintenance ECT treatments every 3–5 weeks to prevent relapse, although few formal studies with maintenance ECT have been reported.

questions.question_text: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) for treatment of which of the following conditions?

options.text: Epilepsy.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Parkinson's disease.
Acute depression.
Chronic pain.

questions.explanation: VNS has been approved since 1997 as a treatment for epilepsy, and was approved by the FDA in 2005 for chronic use in patients with treatment-resistant depression. It is currently being studied for the treatment of anxiety, obesity, and pain.

questions.question_text: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved for which of the following conditions?

options.text: Epilepsy.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Parkinson's disease.
Depression.
Chronic pain.

questions.explanation: DBS has FDA approval for the treatment of Parkinson’s disease. A humanitarian device exemption was granted by the FDA for using DBS in patients with treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder. DBS is also being studied in depression, Tourette’s disorder, substance abuse, addictions, obesity, and schizophrenia
